rounds.Answer:
Extracting the publication date of a webpage is a bit more challenging because there isn't a standard method for websites to display this information. However, there are a few approaches you can try:

Metadata Tags: Some websites use metadata tags within the <head> section of the HTML to specify the publication date. Common tag names include article:published_time, og:published_time, or simply published.

Article Tags: If the webpage follows semantic HTML5 standards, the publication date might be included in an <article> tag, possibly within a <time> element.

URL or Page Content: Occasionally, the publication date is embedded in the URL or visibly displayed on the page. This would require custom parsing logic for each website format.

HTTP Headers: Sometimes, the HTTP headers of the webpage contain a Last-Modified field. This isn't necessarily the publication date but can sometimes serve as a rough estimate.

For a more robust implementation, you might need to combine several of these methods and include fallbacks. Keep in mind that the accuracy of these methods can vary greatly from site to site. Here's an updated version of the fetch_content_from_url function implementing some of these strategies:

def fetch_content_from_url(url)
  response = HTTParty.get(url)
  html = response.body
  parsed_html = Nokogiri::HTML(html)

  title = parsed_html.at('head title')&.text || ''
  description = parsed_html.at('head meta[name="description"]')&.attr('content') || ''
  body_content = parsed_html.at('body')&.inner_html || ''
  published = parse_published_date(parsed_html, response.headers)

  {
    title: title,
    content: body_content,
    summary: description,
    published: published
  }
end

def parse_published_date(parsed_html, headers)
  # Try to extract from metadata
  published_meta = parsed_html.at('head meta[property="article:published_time"], head meta[name="published"], head meta[property="og:published_time"]')&.attr('content')
  return published_meta if published_meta

  # Try to extract from article tag
  published_article = parsed_html.at('article time')&.attr('datetime')
  return published_article if published_article

  # Fallback to Last-Modified header
  headers['Last-Modified'] || Time.now
end

rounds.Prompt: could i combine custom sql test with error_if
rounds.Answer:
Yes, you can absolutely combine a custom SQL test with error_if or warn_if thresholds in dbt. This gives you the ability to control pass/fail behavior based on numeric thresholds, including percentages, without raising an error for every single row.

✅ How error_if works with custom SQL tests

When you write a custom SQL test, dbt expects your query to return 0 rows to pass, and any rows returned will be treated as failures.

The error_if and warn_if thresholds then let you control:

how many rows are allowed before the test fails (error_if)

how many can fail before just issuing a warning (warn_if)

🚫 Limitation: thresholds are based on row counts, not percentages

However, error_if only works on row counts, not percentage values in a column. So you can’t say “fail if >5% of rows are bad” directly using error_if, unless you compute the percentage inside your custom SQL test and then return a row only when the threshold is exceeded.

rounds.Prompt: can i use simple machine learning algo to optimize cache hit rate ?
rounds.Answer:
Yes, you can use simple machine learning algorithms to optimize cache hit rates. The key idea is to predict which data or instructions are most likely to be accessed in the near future and keep them in the cache. This process involves analyzing access patterns and making educated guesses about future requests.

Here are a few ways you can use machine learning for cache optimization:

Predictive Caching: Use historical access data to train a model that predicts which items are likely to be accessed in the near future. For instance, algorithms like decision trees or logistic regression can be employed to classify data based on access frequency and recency.

Clustering: Implement clustering algorithms (like K-means) to group similar data items. This approach assumes that items in the same group are likely to be accessed around the same time.

Anomaly Detection: Detect unusual access patterns that might indicate a change in the usage trend. This can help adjust the caching strategy dynamically.

Reinforcement Learning: Apply reinforcement learning where the model learns the optimal caching strategy by receiving feedback on its previous decisions (cache hits and misses).

Time Series Analysis: If the access patterns have a temporal component, time series forecasting models (like ARIMA or LSTM neural networks) can be used to predict future accesses.

It's important to note that while machine learning can improve cache hit rates, it also adds complexity and overhead. The choice of algorithm should balance the accuracy of predictions with the computational cost of running the model. Additionally, the model needs to be retrained periodically to adapt to changing access patterns.

When you run multiple instances of a Kafka consumer script, they will consume messages from the same topic independently by default. If you want to share the load of consuming messages from the same topic across multiple consumer instances, you need to make sure they are part of the same consumer group.

In Apache Kafka, consumers can be part of consumer groups, and each group can consume from one or more topics. Kafka ensures that the messages from a particular topic are distributed among the consumers in the same consumer group in a load-balanced manner. Each message is consumed by only one consumer within a group.

Here's how you can modify your Kafka consumer script to make it part of a consumer group:

Update the group.id property in your configuration to specify the same consumer group ID for all your consumer instances. This is important to ensure that they belong to the same group.

You can add an additional --group-id argument to your script to specify the consumer group ID from the command line. This way, you can run multiple consumer instances with different group IDs if needed.

rounds.Prompt: Is it possible to get the second page of Hacker News via API? I think it may not be, I think the official algolia API only has a front_page tag for things on the front page right now
rounds.Answer:
Short answer: no—the Algolia “front_page” endpoint only ever gives you the current front‑page set (30 hits by default, up to 50 if you bump hitsPerPage). It ignores the page= parameter, so there’s no built‑in way to fetch “page 2”.

Why it works that way

tags=front_page is a snapshot of whatever HN considers the front page right now. The indexer retags stories when they fall off, so it doesn’t store historical pages to paginate through. The best you can do is increase hitsPerPage (e.g. …search_by_date?tags=front_page&hitsPerPage=50) to grab a slightly larger slice, but that’s still one request, not true paging GitHub.

The official Firebase API exposes the 500 IDs currently ranked as “top stories” at /v0/topstories. It’s just an array, so you can paginate client‑side—slice items 0‑29 for page 1, 30‑59 for page 2, and so on—but you’ll have to fetch each item ID to get metadata, and the ranking won’t exactly match the Algolia front page because HN applies a time‑decay algorithm between refreshes GitHub.

What you can do instead

Client‑side pagination with Firebase IDs

GET https://hacker-news.firebaseio.com/v0/topstories.json → array of up to 500 IDs.

Slice it however you like and then request /v0/item/<id>.json for the details.

Approximate with Algolia search (no front_page tag)

Drop tags=front_page and sort by points or date:

https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/search?tags=story&numericFilters=points>50&hitsPerPage=30&page=1

The ordering will differ from the live HN ranking, but you can page through arbitrarily.

Scrape the HTML (least pleasant, but mirrors what the HN web UI does): request https://news.ycombinator.com/news?p=2 and parse the markup.

Key take‑aways

Algolia’s front_page tag is single‑page by design.

If you need deterministic paging, use the Firebase list or scrape the HTML; Algolia has no historical front‑page pagination.

The proposed changes introduce Xef, a programming language designed with a primary focus on AI interactions. The objective of Xef is to seamlessly integrate AI prompts within a programming paradigm.

Features:

AI-Prompts as First-Class Entities:

In the Xef language, system, assistant, and user interactions are embedded within the primary syntax, ensuring AI interactions are inherent to the language structure.

[[CODE_57_0]]

Modular Design:

Xef modules are version-controlled, can be imported, and reused, making the language modular and scalable.

[[CODE_57_1]]

JVM Integration:

Xef can interact with JVM through a simplified import mechanism, allowing for seamless integration of existing JVM libraries.

[[CODE_57_2]]

Concise Control Structures:

[[CODE_57_3]]

Dynamic Inference Mechanism:

Users can utilize placeholders for inferences, offering a way for dynamic interactions with the AI model.

[[CODE_57_4]]

Argument System with Typing:

[[CODE_57_5]]

rounds.Answer:
RSA encryption is a widely-used public key cryptosystem that relies on the mathematical properties of large prime numbers. Here are the steps involved in RSA encryption:

1. Key Generation

a. Select Two Large Prime Numbers

Choose two distinct large prime numbers ppp and qqq.

b. Compute nnn

Compute nnn by multiplying ppp and qqq:

n=p×qn = p \times qn=p×q

c. Compute Euler's Totient Function ϕ(n)\phi(n)ϕ(n)

Calculate ϕ(n)\phi(n)ϕ(n) (also known as Euler's totient function):

ϕ(n)=(p−1)×(q−1)\phi(n) = (p - 1) \times (q - 1)ϕ(n)=(p−1)×(q−1)

d. Choose the Public Exponent eee

Select an integer eee such that 1<e<ϕ(n)1 < e < \phi(n)1<e<ϕ(n) and gcd(e,ϕ(n))=1\text{gcd}(e, \phi(n)) = 1gcd(e,ϕ(n))=1. This means eee and ϕ(n)\phi(n)ϕ(n) are coprime.

e. Compute the Private Exponent ddd

Compute ddd as the modular multiplicative inverse of eee modulo ϕ(n)\phi(n)ϕ(n):

d×e≡1 (mod ϕ(n))d \times e \equiv 1 \ (\text{mod} \ \phi(n))d×e≡1 (mod ϕ(n))

2. Public and Private Keys

The public key is the pair (e,n)(e, n)(e,n).

The private key is the pair (d,n)(d, n)(d,n).

3. Encryption

a. Convert the Message to a Number

Represent the plaintext message MMM as an integer mmm such that 0≤m<n0 \leq m < n0≤m<n.

b. Encrypt the Message

Compute the ciphertext ccc using the public key (e,n)(e, n)(e,n):

c=me (mod n)c = m^e \ (\text{mod} \ n)c=me (mod n)

4. Decryption

a. Decrypt the Ciphertext

Compute the original message mmm from the ciphertext ccc using the private key (d,n)(d, n)(d,n):

m=cd (mod n)m = c^d \ (\text{mod} \ n)m=cd (mod n)

Summary

Key Generation: Generate ppp, qqq, nnn, ϕ(n)\phi(n)ϕ(n), eee, and ddd.

Encryption: Convert message to integer mmm and compute c=me (mod n)c = m^e \ (\text{mod} \ n)c=me (mod n).

Decryption: Compute m=cd (mod n)m = c^d \ (\text{mod} \ n)m=cd (mod n).

By following these steps, RSA encryption and decryption ensure secure communication. The security of RSA relies on the computational difficulty of factoring the large number nnn into its prime components ppp and qqq.

When generating the RSA keys:

def extended_gcd(a, b):
    if b == 0:
        return a, 1, 0
    gcd, x1, y1 = extended_gcd(b, a % b)

    y = x1 - (a // b) * y1

def modular_inverse(e, phi_n):
    gcd, x, _ = extended_gcd(e, phi_n)
    if gcd == 1:

macOS uses a complex font fallback mechanism. If it can’t find a glyph in your chosen font, it falls back to other system fonts—sometimes CJK fonts (Chinese/Japanese/Korean), which contain many ambiguous Unicode symbols that overlap with Nerd Font icons (especially in the Private Use Area).

The fallback font order

rounds.Prompt: How many Python objects are round-trip serializable between their __str__ method. Is it common?
rounds.Answer:
In Python, the primary purpose of the __str__ method is to provide a human-readable string representation of an object, and it is not designed for serialization-deserialization purposes. Serialization usually refers to the process of converting an object into a format that can be easily stored or transmitted and then reconstructed later. The common formats for serialization in Python are JSON, XML, or using Python's built-in pickle module.

The idea of "round-trip serialization" using the __str__ method would imply that an object can be converted to a string using __str__ and then reconstructed back to its original state from this string. This is generally not feasible with the __str__ method for several reasons:

Loss of Information: The __str__ method often does not contain all the information necessary to recreate the object. It typically provides a summary or a simplified representation that's useful for logging or debugging, but not for full reconstruction.

Format and Parsing: Even if __str__ includes all the necessary information about an object, parsing this information back into an object would require a custom parser. Python does not provide a built-in way to automatically reverse the output of __str__ back into an object.

Complex Data Types: For complex data types and objects containing other objects, the __str__ method would become increasingly complex and inefficient if it were to include comprehensive serialization information.

In Python, if you need to serialize and deserialize objects, it is more common and advisable to use:

pickle: For Python-specific binary serialization, which handles a wide array of Python objects automatically.

JSON (with custom encoding/decoding): For text-based serialization when interoperability with other systems (e.g., web applications) is necessary. Custom encoders and decoders can be written for objects.

Here's an example using pickle for serialization and deserialization:

[[CODE_3_0]]
This example uses pickle to serialize a Person object into a byte stream and then deserialize it back into a Python object, preserving all attributes and their states. This approach is much more robust and reliable than attempting to use __str__ for the same purpose.

Determining if a class has a "good" __repr__ method can be somewhat subjective, as it depends on the intended use and context. However, there are general principles and best practices that can guide the evaluation of whether a __repr__ method is well-implemented:

1. Clarity and Completeness

A good __repr__ should provide a clear and complete representation of the object’s state. It ideally includes all information necessary to understand the object or to recreate it, which can be particularly useful during debugging. If you can look at the __repr__ output and get a full understanding of the object's state, it’s a good sign.

2. Valid Python Expression

One common guideline for __repr__ is that it should, as much as possible, return a string that looks like a valid Python expression that could be used to recreate the object. This is not always feasible, especially for complex objects, but it’s a useful goal. For example:

3. Consistency

The representation should be consistent in format, which helps in understanding and using the output programmatically if needed. Consistency is particularly important when the object is part of a collection or when objects of the class are frequently logged or monitored.

4. Performance

While not usually a primary concern, __repr__ should not be overly complex or perform heavy computations, as it might be called frequently (such as when objects are printed in a list). The method should be efficient enough not to negatively impact performance unexpectedly.

5. Safety

Ensure that calling __repr__ does not have side effects which alter the state of the object. __repr__ should be safe to call at any point without modifying how the object behaves.

Practical Evaluation:

To evaluate whether a class has a good __repr__, consider the following:

Does it include all critical attributes of the object?

Is the output helpful for debugging (i.e., can a developer understand what the object represents just by seeing its __repr__ output)?

# ✨The Reselling Search API✨:

I am the creator of [Saddlebag Exchange](https://saddlebagexchange.com/), where our open source community has been building free API marketboard tools based off of [Universalis](https://universalis.app/) data for over 2 years!

Based [on our previous post about our new public documentation](https://www.reddit.com/r/ffxiv/comments/1hb36fm/new_ffxiv_economy_api_documentation_available/) we are going to be making series of posts this year to describe each of our APIs in more detail.

We will start our with our most popular tool the [Reselling search](https://saddlebagexchange.com/queries/recommended)! This is a unique tool used to find the best items to buy from other servers or from vendors and sell on your own home server for a profit!

🔗 You can view our web page for the [Reselling search here.](https://saddlebagexchange.com/queries/recommended)

🔗 You can view and try the [API directly within our Documentation site here.](https://docs.saddlebagexchange.com/redoc#operation/ffxiv_reselling_api_scan_post)

I also would recommend [CodeRabbit](https://www.coderabbit.ai/) and [Cursor](https://www.cursor.com/) which really helped me get this documentation together using FastAPI docs.

# 🛠️ Parameter Overview:

We are going to be a bit technical here and try to go into detail on what all of our parameters mean and are intended for.  Please let us know if you want more detail in the comments below.

* `preferred_roi`: Sets the Desired Return on Investment (ROI) percentage. For example, a value of 25 means aiming for a 25% profit or better (e.g. finding an item for 75,000 gil profit that you can sell for 100,000 gil or more).
* `min_profit_amount`: Sets the Minimum profit in gil per item. For instance, 100,000 gil ensures the results only include items you can resell for at least 100k profit.
* `min_desired_avg_ppu`: Minimum average price per unit in gil. Limits the search results to items averaging this price or higher based on previous recent sales on your server.
* `min_stack_size`: Minimum quantity of an item to consider. For example, a value of 2 ignores single-item listings, it removes items like gear or furnishings, focusing on commodities like materia.
* `hours_ago`: Time frame in hours for analyzing sales data. For example, you can set this to look over the past 168 hours of sales to see a one week cycle or set this to 24 hours to see what is selling the fastest!
* `min_sales`: Minimum number of sales within the specified `hours_ago` period. This is used for sale rate calculations and it insures the search results only contain data on items actually selling. For example, if you set the `min_sales` to 7 and the `hours_ago` to 168 then you will get items that sell at least once per day.
* `hq`: Filters the results to include only high-quality (HQ) items if set to `True`.
* `home_server`: Name of your home server where items will be sold. Sales statistics are based on this server.
* `filters`: Allows you to list of category and subcategory IDs to filter items. We use this to create more specialized searches such as our [furnishings search](https://saddlebagexchange.com/queries/full-scan?hours=168&salesAmount=2&ROI=25&minimumStackSize=1&minimumProfitAmount=75000&pricePerUnit=30000&filters=56,65,66,67,68,69,70,71,72,81,82&hQChecked=false&includeVendorChecked=true&outOfStockChecked=true&regionWideChecked=true) or our [consumable and collectibles search.](https://saddlebagexchange.com/queries/full-scan?hours=168&salesAmount=2&ROI=25&minimumStackSize=1&minimumProfitAmount=75000&pricePerUnit=30000&filters=75,80,90&hQChecked=false&includeVendorChecked=true&outOfStockChecked=true&regionWideChecked=true)
* `region_wide`: If `True`, search across all data centers in your region; if `False`, the tool only searches your specific data center.
* `include_vendor`: Include vendor prices in the search results as if vendors were another server when set to `True`.  This is set to false by default when you search for `hq` items.
* `show_out_stock`: Display out-of-stock items in search results if set to `True`; otherwise, show only currently available items.  Some prefer this option as out of stock items can often have old data.

# 🛠️ Results Overview:

rounds.Answer:
Best practice (SEO-safe) is not to redirect at all — instead serve the “About/marketing” HTML at betarena.com/ for logged-out users, and keep the app for logged-in users. That avoids crawler mismatches, link equity fragmentation, and “cloaking” accusations.

If you must redirect to about.betarena.com, do it like this:

Option A (recommended): No redirect, swap content by auth

Goal: betarena.com/ returns:

Logged-in → app

Logged-out → the same marketing page content (you can proxy/serve the same build you host on about.betarena.com)

Why it’s safest

Crawlers see a normal 200 page (no redirect chains).

No “bot sees X / users see Y” redirect behavior.

You can keep one canonical root domain for SEO.

How

At the edge (Cloudflare Worker), check your auth cookie/session.

If missing, respond with marketing HTML (or proxy fetch from about.betarena.com and return it).

Make sure caching is private or varies by cookie.

Option B: Redirect logged-out humans, but keep crawlers clean

If you still want redirect:

Rules

Only redirect HTML navigations

GET requests

Accept contains text/html

Do not redirect API/assets (/api, /assets, fonts, images, /_app, etc.)

Do NOT redirect verified/known crawlers

Use Cloudflare Bot Management if you have it: request.cf.botManagement.verifiedBot

If not, fallback to allowlist user agents (Googlebot, Bingbot, etc.) and ideally reverse-DNS verification (harder).

Use a temporary redirect:

302 (or 307) for logged-out users.

Avoid 301 unless you truly want Google to treat this as permanent site move for those URLs.

Avoid redirect loops and give an escape hatch:

Don’t redirect requests already on about.betarena.com

Optional: ?noredirect=1 for debugging/support.

Keep SEO signals consistent

On about.betarena.com, set canonical carefully.

If about.betarena.com is just a “public brochure”, I’d typically canonical it to itself (not to betarena.com) unless you’re also serving that same brochure at betarena.com/ (Option A). Duplicates can get messy.

Minimal Worker logic (concept)

If no auth cookie AND HTML navigation AND not verified bot → 302 to https://about.betarena.com/

Else → pass through

Quick warning

Redirecting humans but not crawlers can look like cloaking if the crawler can’t reproduce what a user sees. That’s why Option A (serve brochure at betarena.com/ for logged-out) is the cleanest.

The errors you're seeing are due to missing standard C++ library symbols, which typically occur when the linker is not correctly linking against the C++ standard library. This can happen when using lld with Clang, particularly when combining LTO (Link Time Optimization) with -flto.

Run the Makefile:

Use the make command to build the project: make.
